examples.text: When rain hits a gabi leaf, it forms tiny round beads of water that roll right off instead of soaking in.
Tinapa is fish cooked and dried over smoke! The smoke gives it a special flavor and helps it last longer.
Science starts with good questions like 'Why?' and 'How?' — they push us to investigate and search for answers.
With your teacher, ask: can folded paper stand up? Try folding a sheet, test it on the table, and change the fold. Describe what happened. Asking and trying materials are parts of science.

A ruler is a handy tool for measuring length! It has centimeter and millimeter marks to show exactly how long an object is.

Why do scientists use a hand lens or ruler when they already have eyes?

Because tools like hand lenses and rulers extend the senses! They help us see tiny details and measure length more accurately than our eyes alone.
Scissors are used to cut cloth, paper, cardboard, and other thin materials.
With your teacher, compare an empty balloon with an inflated one. A balloon stretches as air goes inside. It helps you observe that air takes up space.
Modeling clay can be pressed and shaped into simple models during a science activity. You can reshape the same clay to compare a ball with a flat shape.

How can small pieces of cardboard become one big useful thing?

When you join pieces with tape or glue, they stick together and form a larger, stronger object. Joining changes the size and shape of the material!

How do scientists observe carefully?

They look, listen, and touch carefully! Then, they write down exactly what they notice without adding any guesses.

How do scientists predict and check?

They use what they know to guess what happens next in a test, then they measure to check!
Look closely at your ruler! One centimeter equals exactly 10 millimeters. Count them yourself!

With your teacher, place a pencil beside a ruler. Line up one end with the zero mark and read the other end at eye level. Record the length and unit. A pencil reaching 12 cm is 120 mm long because 1 cm = 10 mm. Use a meter stick or tape for longer lengths: 1 m = 100 cm.
The symbol for centimeter is "cm"! You see it all the time on your school rulers.

With your teacher, place a pencil beside a ruler. Line up one end with the zero mark and read the other end at eye level. Record the length and unit. A pencil reaching 12 cm is 120 mm long because 1 cm = 10 mm. Use a meter stick or tape for longer lengths: 1 m = 100 cm.
One meter equals exactly 100 centimeters! You can fit 100 small centimeters inside one big meter.

The hardness of a mineral simply means how hard it is to scratch!

What do we call the bright, shiny surface of clean metals?

Metals are usually shiny, and their bright surface is called a metallic luster when they are clean!

What happens when you blow into a balloon?

It fills with air, which is a gas! The rubber stretches to hold all that air inside.
Recycling reduces pollution! When we recycle, less trash is burned or left in nature to harm our air and water.
Burning dried leaves releases fine particulate matter into the air! Avoid breathing it in to prevent coughing and asthma attacks.
Throwing trash like plastic anywhere clogs drains and waterways! Because rainwater cannot flow, flooding happens.

How can we help reduce pollution?

Buy less plastic and reuse what we already have!

Why can't we pour used cooking oil down the sink?

Oil can clog the pipes and harm the environment, so it should be sealed in a container and thrown in the garbage.

With your teacher, sort clean paper, plastic containers, and intact bottles for reuse or recycling. Follow the local collection rules. Keep away from broken glass and ask an adult to collect it safely. An adult should cool used cooking oil, seal it in a container, and use the local disposal or collection service; never pour it down a drain.
Recycling means making new things out of old waste, like making new paper from used paper!
Always separate your paper from other trash! Putting it in its own bin makes it super easy to recycle.

Did you know shape matters? A sinking ball of clay can actually float when you shape it like a bowl!
The paper in your notebook is made from tiny wood fibers mashed into pulp, pressed flat, and dried!
Metals are malleable — you can bend or hammer them into new shapes without breaking!
An anvil is a heavy, solid metal tool! It provides a hard surface for hammering and shaping other heated metals.

How can small pieces of cardboard become one big useful thing?

When you join pieces with tape or glue, they stick together and form a larger, stronger object. Joining changes the size and shape of the material!
The hard trunk of an old coconut tree is cut into "coco lumber," used as posts and boards for building houses.
Steel is a super strong alloy made of iron mixed with just a small amount of carbon!
Iron is a super strong metal! We use it to build tall buildings, big bridges, and vehicles.
Gold is a shiny, valuable metal! We use it to make beautiful jewelry like rings and necklaces.
Long ago, people used silver as money and coins because it was super valuable and easy to carry around!
Malleable materials can be hammered and formed into shapes, like gold and silver being made into jewelry.
The wires in your house are made of copper because it conducts electricity super well!
Observing is a science process skill that uses your senses to describe things around you.

With your teacher, observe a small plant and measure its height in centimeters. Predict whether it will grow taller. Care for it normally, then measure again after several days. Record both heights and compare your prediction with what you observed.
Predicting is a science process skill where you use careful observations and patterns to make a smart guess about what will happen next.

With your teacher, observe a small plant and measure its height in centimeters. Predict whether it will grow taller. Care for it normally, then measure again after several days. Record both heights and compare your prediction with what you observed.
Measuring is a science process skill that uses units like millimeters, centimeters, and meters to describe the size of objects.

A carabao pulls a wooden cart — are they both alive?

Nope! The carabao eating grass is living, but the wooden cart is non-living — it can't eat or grow!

Is coral a rock or a plant?

Neither! Coral is actually made of tiny living animals called polyps.

Is coral a rock?

No -- coral is a living animal! Each tiny polyp has a mouth and tentacles to catch food; the hard part is just the house it builds around itself.
Living things grow and change over time, like a seed becoming a plant or a puppy becoming a dog.

How does one rice seedling become a bush?

From just one seedling, a rice plant grows many stems, until the single plant becomes a full, bushy clump.
It's not just touch — strong wind, raindrops, or heat can also make makahiya's leaves fold, since it reacts to any sudden disturbance.
Some animals, like chickens and other birds, make babies by laying eggs.
A frog's strong, long back legs are what let it jump so far!
A crab has ten legs in total — eight for walking and two that are pincer claws!
Many insects have wings that let them fly through the air.
Swifts have long, narrow wings shaped perfectly for flying very fast.
A bird's beak shape matches the kind of food it eats!
Cats and dogs both have sharp teeth built for eating meat.
Rats use their long tail to keep their balance while climbing.
Milkfish are strong, fast swimmers thanks to their wide, forked tail.
Roots soak up water and nutrients from the soil so the plant can stay alive and grow.
A plant's roots soak up water and nutrients from the soil so the whole plant can use them.
The stem carries water up from the roots all the way to the leaves.

What is a tree's trunk, really?

It's actually one giant, hard stem — strong enough to support the whole tree!
The green leaves of a rice plant use sunlight to make their own food.
Just like other plants, an orchid makes its own food using its green leaves and sunlight.
A seed needs three things to sprout: water, warmth, and air.
All animals, including us humans, need oxygen to stay alive.
Hunger goes away when you eat enough food.
Dogs need clean food, fresh water, and good care to stay healthy.
A seed needs three things to sprout: water, warmth, and air.
Your skin keeps water inside your body so you don't dry out.
Cloud rats shelter and rest in holes or hollows inside old, large trees.
A coral reef is a home and shelter for many fish and other sea creatures.
A koala eats almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves.
Chickens eat grains, seeds, insects, and small worms.
To grow tall and healthy, corn needs sunlight, water, and good soil.
A goat is a farm animal that people raise for its milk, meat, and hair.
Restored forests help store clean water in streams and watersheds.
Planting narra trees helps bring back forests that have been cut down.
Restored forests help store clean water in streams and watersheds.

A wind turbine spins when the wind blows, and that spinning motion generates electricity!

What happens when wind pushes against a turbine's blades?

The blades spin and turn the machine!
A river current spins a water wheel on its axle, transferring power to grind grain in a mill!
Flowing water has a strong force that can push things, just like how it can turn a water wheel!
You use a push when you close a door or push a cart!
When you push or pull a door open, you are using force in both actions!
When you push or pull a door open, you are using force in both actions!
Farmers use the carabao to pull a plow and break up the soil in rice fields.
A cargo tricycle rolls forward when its engine burns fuel to power the turning wheels!
A kalesa is a carriage pulled by a horse—the horse uses muscle power to apply force and make the wheels roll!
People can move objects by pushing, pulling, carrying, lifting, or blowing on them.
Carrying means holding an object while moving, like when you hug a book and walk to your seat.

With your teacher, compare how objects move. First record size, shape, mass and material. To test surface texture, roll the same ball from the same ramp mark onto smooth cloth and rough cloth; measure how far it goes. Change only the cloth. To test mass, keep the toy car, ramp and surface the same but add a small load. Do not blame size alone when material or mass also changes.
A larger size does not always mean a bigger mass; a bowling ball has more matter packed inside it than a football of the same size.

Playing sungka on a smooth wooden board reduces friction, allowing the little shells to slide easily right into the holes!
A ball rolling on grass stops faster than on smooth tile! The rough grass creates more friction to slow it down.
Ice is super slippery because it has very little friction! This makes it the perfect surface to skate or slide on.
Objects can move closer to or farther from their original position in relation to a reference point.
Objects can move to the left or to the right in relation to their original position.
To measure distance, mark the starting position and final position of a moving object, then use a ruler or tape measure to find the length between them.
A drum makes sound because its stretched skin vibrates when you strike it!
Sound is actually a vibration! It travels through the air and enters your ear so you can hear it.
Sound needs a material to travel through — like air, water, or a solid. No material means no sound!
The sun is actually a giant star! It is Earth's main source of light and heat, keeping our planet warm and bright.
Candles and flashlights both give light! A candle burns wax to make a hot flame, while a flashlight uses battery electricity, making it safer with no flame.

How do we see an object?

We see it when light bounces off the object and enters our eyes!
Indoors, you can make a shadow using a flashlight and an object that blocks its light!
Without light there is no shadow; light is needed for a shadow to exist!
Very loud sounds can damage the tiny parts inside your ear and weaken your hearing.
Ultraviolet light from the sun causes sunburn, which makes our skin turn red and get damaged!
Never shine a laser pointer into eyes! Even a small, cheap laser can injure the eye's retina.
Raising or lowering a colored flag is a movement-and-color signal! People use it so a far partner can easily see a yes or a no.

With your teacher, agree with a partner that one wave, soft clap, or flashlight blink means yes and two mean no. Send a message from 5 meters away. Aim the flashlight at a wall, never at eyes. Ask the partner to decode it, record whether it worked, and change one part if it was unclear. Test again.
In a tin-can telephone, sound travels along the tight string as vibrations — like a secret message highway!

Two people can send information with a flashlight! Just agree that one blink means yes and two blinks mean no, even when too far to talk.

How are ceramics made?

Ceramics are made from clay! The clay is first shaped, and then it is baked in fire.

What is a palayok used for?

Clay pots made of ceramic have long been used in the Philippines for cooking food!
Air is an earth material you can't hold like a pebble, but it fills the space around every living thing!
Clay is a sticky earth material made of tiny mineral bits. It's non-living, even when people shape it into pots!
A weather chart tracks if it's sunny, rainy, or cloudy every day, helping us spot patterns in the weather!
A weather chart tracks if it's sunny, rainy, or cloudy every day, helping us spot patterns in the weather!

Why is it warmer during the day and cooler at night?

It is warmer when the Sun is up during the day, and cooler at night!
Observing the weather condition helps us decide the kind of activities we will do for the day, like playing outside or staying indoors.
Heavy monsoon rains often cause rapid flash floods in low-lying areas of Metro Manila!

Can we only see the Moon at night?

Nope! Sometimes, we can also see the Moon in the bright daytime sky!

With an adult, observe from the same safe place at different times. Draw the Moon, visible stars, or a planet identified with a sky chart beside a fixed landmark. Write the date and time, then compare their positions. Some objects may be hidden by clouds or below the horizon. Track the Sun using a stick’s shadow; never look directly at the Sun.
Earth's only moon has a simple name: we just call it the Moon, or Luna!

You can spot five planets with just your eyes — no telescope needed! They are Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.

The nearest star to Earth is our very own Sun!

You can record the Sun's apparent movement safely by marking the shadow of a stick on the ground at different times, without looking directly at the Sun.
Just like the Sun, the Moon rises in the east and sets in the west because of Earth's rotation!

Why does the sun look like it's moving across our sky?

In the Philippines, the sun appears to move because the Earth rotates on its axis!
A sundial is a super cool ancient clock that tells time just by using the shadow cast by the sun!
Lost at night? Look up for the North Star, Polaris! It points to true north to help you navigate back safely.
Before the compass, sailors used stars and constellations to find direction on the open sea at night! They followed stars pointing north or south.
Too much sun can burn your skin — that's why wearing a hat or sunblock outside is so important!

How can clothes protect your skin from the Sun?

A long-sleeve shirt or wrap covers your skin! This clothing safety measure stops so much of the Sun's light from reaching it.

Why shouldn't we stare at the sun?

We should never stare straight at the sun because it can damage our eyes!
